title: SYSK Selects: Can Your Grandfather's Diet Shorten Your Life?
summary: A Stuff You Should Know Selects episode (originally published from a June 2010 topic) on epigenetics: how chemical "methyl tags" switch genes on and off without changing DNA, and how diet, stress, abuse, and smoking may affect later generations. Covers honey bee queen development, the agouti (goody) mouse experiments, the Swedish Överkalix famine records and grandchildren's lifespans, Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes and genomic imprinting, PTSD in children of mothers pregnant during 9/11, possible medical uses such as cancer and leukemia treatment with drugs like azacitidine, the Human Epigenome Project, and skeptical comments about Bruce Lipton. Includes a listener mail segment from a young fan named Sarah.

segments.title: Cold open and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts tease the episode on whether a grandfather's diet can shorten a grandchild's life, then introduce epigenetics with a brief comparison of Darwin and Lamarck.

segments.title: Genome versus epigenome
segments.summary: The epigenome is compared to software running on genome hardware. All cells share the same DNA, and methyl tags on genes determine which are switched on or off, making a cell a fingernail cell, neuron, or sperm cell.

segments.title: Honey bee queens and mouse coat color
segments.summary: Royal jelly adds a methyl tag to a gene in queen bee larvae, turning off the default worker pathway. In agouti mice, methylation changes body size, weight, and coat color, and maternal B vitamin diet changes offspring.

segments.title: Nature, nurture, and transmission to children
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how environmental factors such as diet, stress and exercise may alter gene expression and affect children and grandchildren, framing epigenetics as a nature-versus-nurture answer.

segments.title: Swedish famine and grandchildren's lifespan
segments.summary: Researcher Lars-Olov Bygren studied agricultural records from an isolated Swedish town. Grandchildren of men who experienced feast or famine within a year of each other lived on average about 32 years less than grandchildren of men without that experience.

segments.title: Genomic imprinting: Angelman and Prader-Willi
segments.summary: Missing DNA segments cause Angelman syndrome or Prader-Willi syndrome depending on which parent the segment came from, a pattern explained by genomic imprinting. The hosts note this is a recent field, with foundations laid in the mid-to-late 1990s.

segments.title: PTSD, stress, and mouse parenting
segments.summary: A study of pregnant women in New York during 9/11 found their babies had lower cortisol levels, suggesting inherited stress response. Mice raised by stressed mothers were jumpy, which the hosts theorize is an adaptive epigenetic change. Methyl tags may fade over several generations.

segments.title: Medical potential: cancer and leukemia
segments.summary: Epigenetic switches may be easier to change than cancer cells directly. A drug originally marketed for another purpose was found to turn down growth genes and was used for leukemia, with some patients entering remission.

segments.title: Smoking, cocaine, and the Human Epigenome Project
segments.summary: Smoking before puberty was linked to shorter, fatter, less healthy children in a study of Swedish fathers, and cocaine was linked to memory problems in offspring of mice. The Human Epigenome Project is described as far larger in scope than the Human Genome Project.

segments.title: Skeptical take on Bruce Lipton and mind over genes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Bruce Lipton's claim that the mind can alter the epigenome, relating it to the placebo effect and spontaneous remission, and note that he is viewed as controversial. They suggest stress reduction as a more plausible mechanism.

segments.title: Further resources
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the University of Utah epigenetics website, the PBS program The Ghost in Your Genes, and a HowStuffWorks article on epigenetics.

segments.title: Listener mail from Sarah
segments.summary: A young fan named Sarah, now thirteen, emails about her birthday, Lego bricks, and her blog about Australian commercials. The hosts read her message and sign off with encouragement to send in listener mail.
